cases.title: Infected obstructed collecting system
cases.stem: A septic patient has an obstructing ureteric calculus with hydronephrosis. Retrograde ureteric drainage has failed.

questions.question: What is the immediate interventional priority?
questions.explanation: An infected obstructed collecting system requires urgent decompression.

questions.question: Which access trajectory is generally preferred to reduce vascular injury and facilitate drainage?
options: A suitable posterior calyx through renal parenchyma
Direct puncture through the renal hilum
Traversal of the main renal artery
questions.explanation: A posterior calyceal approach usually provides a relatively avascular and practical access path.

questions.question: Which manoeuvre should be avoided in an infected obstructed system?
options: High-pressure injection of large volumes of contrast
questions.explanation: Overpressurisation may force infected material into the circulation and worsen sepsis.

questions.question: Once the patient is stabilised, definitive treatment of the obstructing cause should:
options: Be planned subsequently according to urological and clinical factors
Always precede drainage in a septic patient
questions.explanation: Source control by drainage comes first; definitive stone treatment is usually performed after stabilisation.

cases.title: Percutaneous drainage of a liver abscess
cases.stem: A febrile patient has an 8-cm hepatic abscess that is safely accessible percutaneously and there is no immediate surgical indication.

questions.question: What is the usual image-guided treatment?
questions.explanation: Large accessible abscesses are commonly managed with image-guided catheter drainage plus appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

questions.question: What should be assessed before puncture?
options: A safe route avoiding pleura, bowel and major vessels where possible
questions.explanation: Trajectory planning is essential to minimise transgression of vulnerable structures.

questions.question: If the abscess content is very viscous, management may require:
options: An appropriately sized catheter and protocolised flushing
questions.explanation: Viscous material may require a larger catheter and careful catheter maintenance.

questions.question: When is catheter removal usually considered?
options: Clinical improvement, minimal output and adequate resolution of the cavity in context
Persistent sepsis with a large residual cavity
questions.explanation: Removal is based on clinical recovery, drain output and imaging evidence of adequate resolution.

questions.question: A typical indication for percutaneous cholecystostomy is:
options: Acute cholecystitis in a high-risk patient who is not an immediate surgical candidate
questions.explanation: Cholecystostomy can provide source control in selected high-risk patients.

questions.question: A transhepatic route for cholecystostomy may offer:
options: Improved catheter stability in selected patients
questions.explanation: The transhepatic track can improve stability, although it has its own bleeding risks.

questions.question: The most frequent complication of percutaneous lung biopsy is:
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is common after transthoracic needle biopsy.

questions.question: Which is an important contraindication to vertebroplasty/cement augmentation?
options: Active infection at the target level
questions.explanation: Active infection can lead to severe infectious complications and must be treated first.

questions.question: Hydrodissection during renal tumour ablation is used to:
options: Displace and protect bowel or other heat-sensitive structures
questions.explanation: Creating a fluid plane can increase the distance between the ablation zone and vulnerable structures.

questions.question: A useful feature of cryoablation is that imaging can show:
questions.explanation: The visible ice ball helps monitor treatment extent and adjacent structures.

questions.question: Pre-operative embolisation of a hypervascular tumour may be performed to:
options: Reduce operative blood loss in selected cases
Avoid histological diagnosis in every case
questions.explanation: Pre-operative devascularisation can facilitate surgery for selected hypervascular tumours.

questions.question: Before a deep percutaneous puncture, it is essential to:
options: Review coagulation status and antithrombotic medication
Ignore renal function in every patient
questions.explanation: Bleeding risk should be assessed and antithrombotic management individualised.
